preamble: A special puzzle to mark a weekend anniversary

clue.text: Astronaut Glenn aims to re-enter extremely dramatically

indicators.note: doing something dramatically suggests wild upheaval, so the gathered letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremities of the next word, its first and last letters only

parts.note: the first and last letters of the hyphenated word

explanation.surface: Fellow astronaut John Glenn plans a theatrical return through the atmosphere.
explanation.walkthrough: John Glenn was the first American to orbit the Earth, so he looks like the subject, but his name is only letters. The answer is NEIL ARMSTRONG, first man on the moon in July 1969.
explanation.definitionFit: He was the American commander of Apollo 11 who first walked on the lunar surface.

clue.text: Painter returning from greengrocer gleefully

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the run of letters is read right to left
from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow, lying inside them

parts.note: a run of letters straddling the two words, ending in the first three of the second

explanation.surface: An artist comes home from a cheerful visit to the greengrocer.
explanation.walkthrough: Read greenGROCER GLEefully backwards and EL GRECO appears across the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: El Greco was the Cretan-born Renaissance artist who worked in Toledo, Spain.

clue.text: Mentally derail nut with influence of the moon

indicators.note: mentally hints at a disturbed mind, so the following letters lose their sane order

parts.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A madman goes off the rails, as though the full moon were working on him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mentally' and 'nut' together paint a lunatic, an apt picture since lunacy was once blamed on the moon.
explanation.definitionFit: The rise and fall of the sea caused by lunar gravity is exactly the moon's pull on the oceans.

clue.text: Enter at speed and arrest

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to come in running
second meaning: informal for taking someone into police custody

explanation.surface: Police burst through a door and seize a suspect.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both dashing inside and, colloquially, a police officer detaining a suspect.

clue.text: 'Balanced' lunatic emits cry about first sign of moon

indicators.note: about means around, so the rearranged letters wrap around the single letter
a lunatic is crazed, so the words that follow come out in a crazed order

parts.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: the first sign of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A madman howls at the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lunatic' comes from luna, the moon, which suits the picture; the letters of EMITS CRY rearranged wrap around M.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with matching halves on either side of a line is even and in proportion.

clue.text: Space, they say, is cold

indicators.note: they say means as people pronounce it, so the word is judged on its sound

parts.note: room is space to move in; the word sounding the same is spelt differently

explanation.surface: Folk remark that outer space is freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: In a space-themed puzzle 'Space' suggests the cosmos, but it is the room in a house.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheum is the watery mucus of the eyes or nose, the discharge of a head cold, so it stands for a chill.

clue.text: Put heads together for veggie dish

indicators.note: together says two words are placed side by side to make one

parts.note: two slang words for a head, nut and loaf (from rhyming slang loaf of bread)

explanation.surface: Colleagues confer to plan a vegetarian menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put heads together' is the idiom for consulting; here it is literal, two words for head joined. Loaf is Cockney rhyming slang: loaf of bread, head.
explanation.definitionFit: A nut loaf is a baked savoury loaf of chopped nuts, a classic vegetarian main course.

clue.text: Pinnacle: men of America walked out with message from 1

indicators.note: out means disordered or not in place, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: At their peak of achievement, American spacemen stepped out onto the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a headline about the landing, but all five words before 'out' are letters to rearrange. The message from 1 (Neil Armstrong) is the plaque the crew left: WE CAME IN PEACE FOR ALL MANKIND.
explanation.definitionFit: These words are engraved on the plaque left on the lunar surface by the Apollo 11 crew, signed by Armstrong.

clue.text: See 8
Horse beset by frantic one with spur

indicators.note: beset by means surrounded on all sides, so one piece goes inside the other
frantic means agitated and wild, so the word that follows is jumbled

parts.note: the three letters to be rearranged
gee-gee is a child's word for a horse, written GG

explanation.surface: A horse is surrounded by a panicking rider wearing a spur.
explanation.walkthrough: Gee-gee is nursery talk for a horse; 'with spur' looks like part of the rider's kit, but spur is the definition as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To egg someone on is to urge or goad them forward, as a spur urges on a horse.

clue.text: Buzz notably with anaesthetic to suppress

parts.note: an anaesthetic is something that numbs

indicators.note: to suppress is to hold something down and in, so one piece is kept inside another

parts.note: taken as written
W is a common abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: A buzzing sound is notably dulled by applying an anaesthetic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buzz' looks like a noise but is Buzz Aldrin, the second man onto the moon after Armstrong. The anaesthetic is read as 'something that numbs'.
explanation.definitionFit: Aldrin followed Armstrong down the ladder, making him the second in order, the famous deputy.

clue.text: Overcoming resistance, president conducted cosmic expedition's starting points and departure

parts.note: Abe is Abraham Lincoln, the US president

indicators.note: overcoming suggests climbing over and enclosing an obstacle, so one letter is taken into the pieces

parts.note: to run a meeting is to conduct it
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

indicators.note: the starting points of two words are their first letters

parts.note: the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A president defies opposition to lead a voyage into space.
explanation.walkthrough: Abe is Abraham Lincoln, the usual crossword president; the space voyage in the surface is only two initial letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An aberrance is a deviation from the normal course, a straying away from what is expected.

clue.text: Nationalist wanting moon landing: adventure primarily requiring money

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the word is left without one of its letters

parts.note: taken as written
N is the standard abbreviation for Nationalist

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: the opening letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A flag-waving patriot lacks a moon mission, since any such adventure needs cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moon landing' reads as one event, but moon and landing are separate pieces of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Moola (also moolah) is slang for cash, an informal word for funds.

clue.text: Earth gets horrendously toxic article, matter from afar

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for earth in electrical wiring

indicators.note: horrendously suggests something dreadfully messed up, so the next word is scrambled

parts.note: the five letters to be rearranged
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: The planet is hit by some dreadfully poisonous substance from outer space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Matter from afar' suggests meteorites, but it means curiosities from foreign lands.
explanation.definitionFit: Exotica are objects or styles that are strange and come from distant, foreign places.

clue.text: Contrary and tense, I assembled hors d'œuvres

indicators.note: assembled means put together, so the pieces are joined end to end

parts.note: anti means opposed
the past is a grammatical tense
taken as written

explanation.surface: A stubborn, nervous cook prepares the starters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contrary' and 'tense' read as moods of the cook; tense is the grammar term.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasti are the Italian appetisers served before the main meal, the equivalent of French starters.

clue.text: People going into space?

parts.note: surface reading: astronauts heading off into the cosmos
setter's reading: the number of people who will fit into a room

explanation.walkthrough: In a moon-landing puzzle 'space' means the cosmos, but here it is the space of a chamber, filled with people.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means as many people or things as an enclosed room can hold.

clue.text: Visiting the moon — or returned from journey?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the moon has no water, so anyone there stands on terrain without seas
second meaning: back ashore after a voyage at sea

explanation.surface: Is a traveller up on the moon, or back home from the trip?
explanation.walkthrough: The moon's 'seas' are dust plains with no water, so walking there is a whimsical way to be ashore.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means ashore, away from water, whether on the arid lunar plains or after disembarking a ship.

clue.text: Immediately, Soviet leader subdued with worry: 'This is not rocket science!?'

indicators.note: subdued means held down and contained, so a letter is held inside another word

parts.note: now means at once

indicators.note: a word's leader is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
to eat at someone is to worry them, as in what's eating you

explanation.surface: A Soviet space chief, anxious, is quickly quietened by being told the job is easy.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole spoken remark, a fitting joke in a space puzzle; 'worry' is the sense of nagging at someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying a task is not rocket science means it is easy; the idiom for an easy job is no problem at all.

clue.text: Dim son to join forces

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son
to team up is to combine efforts

explanation.surface: A not very bright son enlists alongside others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dim' looks like an adjective for the son, but it is a verb meaning to blur.
explanation.definitionFit: When a window or glasses steam up, condensation clouds them and makes them less clear.

clue.text: Niçoise ingredient?

parts.note: surface reading: something that goes into a salade niçoise, such as tuna or olives
setter's reading: a component of the printed word itself, the little hook under its c

explanation.walkthrough: Salad ingredients spring to mind, but the clue is about the spelling: the c in Niçoise carries a mark beneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the hook-shaped diacritic placed under a c to show it is pronounced as an s.

clue.text: More bananas or more nuts?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: crazier, bananas being slang for mad
second meaning: likewise crazier, nuts also being slang for mad

explanation.walkthrough: Bananas and nuts look like groceries, but both are slang for mad; the moon link is that loony comes from lunatic.
explanation.definitionFit: Loony is informal for crazy, so the comparative describes someone even crazier.

clue.text: In conclusion, this setter has to improve

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: the end is the conclusion
the setter refers to themself as me

explanation.surface: Finally, the compiler admits the puzzle needs some work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In conclusion' looks like a closing phrase, but In is an instruction to put one piece inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct and revise it, making it better.

clue.text: Architectural order seen in sand or ice

indicators.note: seen in says the letters can be spotted lying inside the words that follow

parts.note: a run straddling all three words: the last letter of the first, the second whole, the start of the third

explanation.surface: A building style is glimpsed in sculptures of sand or ice.
explanation.definitionFit: The Doric is the oldest and plainest of the classical Greek column styles.

clue.text: 'Ready to go off!?' 'Ready to go off.' 'Nonsense!'

parts.note: a playful coinage: inclined to pop, about to burst
a gun at cock has its hammer raised, primed to fire

explanation.surface: An exchange of alarmed cries about something set to explode, dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The same phrase appears twice but yields two words: the whimsical one, marked by '!?', and the firearm one.
explanation.definitionFit: Poppycock is a dated but still-used word for foolish talk or rubbish.

clue.text: Sky etc originally passed at Yuri's tremendous velocity

indicators.note: originally means at the origin, so each word gives only its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letters of the five words

explanation.surface: Yuri Gagarin flew past the sky and the like at enormous speed.
explanation.walkthrough: Sky is the British satellite broadcaster, so the definition is subscription channels; Yuri Gagarin was the first man in space.
explanation.definitionFit: Sky and similar subscription services charge viewers to watch their channels, so they are examples of the category.

clue.text: Showed up with spots, ruby-red essentially: unlikely to take a selfie

parts.note: to come is to show up, here in the past tense
a rash is an outbreak of spots

indicators.note: essentially means at its core, so only the central letter is kept

parts.note: the middle letter of the seven

explanation.surface: Someone appeared with a crimson outbreak of spots and would rather not be photographed.
explanation.walkthrough: The spotty, red-faced person in the picture is exactly the kind who avoids the lens.
explanation.definitionFit: A camera-shy person dislikes being photographed, so they would hardly snap a picture of themself.

clue.text: Early on, 1 recalled being in space

indicators.note: recalled suggests calling something back, so the letters run backwards
early on means only the opening stretch is used and the rest is dropped

parts.note: the answer to 1 across

explanation.surface: The astronaut, at the start, remembered being up in space.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the first five letters of NEIL ARMSTRONG, NEILA, and read them backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An extraterrestrial is a creature that lives out among the stars, beyond our planet.

clue.text: Small step among alien surroundings at first: it diverted a generation

indicators.note: at first says which pieces come at the front of the answer, ahead of the rest

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small
a pace is a single step
the aliens of science fiction arrive as raiders from another world

explanation.surface: Armstrong's small step among strange lunar surroundings captivated a whole generation.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls 'one small step' and the moon landing gripping a generation, but the answer is the 1978 arcade game.
explanation.definitionFit: The arcade shooting game was a craze that entertained millions of young players around 1980.
